opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I took away from her book, *The Worlds I See*, is how personal science really is. From the outside we tend to look at ImageNet as a dataset, a benchmark, a turning point in deep learning. But reading her story, you realize it came from a very specific person with a very specific life: an immigrant kid working in her parents' dry-cleaning shop, taking care of her mother's health, and still holding on to this almost stubborn curiosity about how vision and intelligence work. That made me reflect on my own path. The research you end up doing is often shaped by who you are, not just by what's trendy.

The second thing is conviction. When she started ImageNet, many people thought it was a strange thing to spend years on. Collecting and labeling millions of images didn't look like "real" research to a lot of people at the time. She believed that data, at scale, was the missing piece, and she kept going when it wasn't obvious it would pay off. For people like me who work in computer vision now, that's a reminder that the most important contributions sometimes look unglamorous or even unfashionable at first.

In our conversations, what strikes me is that she thinks about AI very much in terms of people. She talks about "human-centered AI," and it isn't just a slogan for her. She cares about who builds the technology, who benefits from it, and how it connects to things like healthcare and education. Researchers, myself included, can get very absorbed in the next model or the next number on a leaderboard. Talking with her pulls you back to the bigger question of why we're doing this at all.

She's also been pushing the idea of spatial intelligence, that the next frontier is understanding and interacting with the 3D physical world, not just language. That resonates with me a lot, because I've always felt vision is not solved just because we have powerful language models. Seeing, and really understanding the world you see, is still a deep open problem. So I'd say she gave me both a historical perspective and a sense of direction. Vision is where a lot of this started, and I think it's still where a lot of the most interesting work is going to happen.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Fei-Fei Li’s story made him reflect on his own path and that her example is a reminder, but does not say hearing stories from her past comforts him when he faces dilemmas or challenges.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

Thank you for having me. Fei-Fei Li's book, *The Worlds I See*, meant a lot to me, partly because I read it at a point when I was thinking hard about what I actually wanted to do as a researcher. I'll try to be honest about what I took from it rather than give a polished answer.

The first thing is that the book is not really a book about AI. It's a book about a person. She writes about moving from Chengdu to New Jersey as a teenager, about her mother's health, about running the family dry-cleaning shop on weekends while she was at Princeton. And then ImageNet shows up almost as a consequence of that life, not as the center of it. That reframed something for me. We tend to tell the history of the field as a sequence of papers and breakthroughs. But the actual story is people with very specific, often difficult circumstances, making bets that looked unreasonable at the time. ImageNet was a bet almost nobody supported. People told her it was a waste of her tenure clock. She did it anyway, and she did it for years before it paid off. I think about that a lot now, because the field is so fast and so crowded, and there's enormous pressure to work on whatever is hot this quarter. Her example says: find the thing you believe is fundamentally missing, and be willing to be lonely for a while.

The second thing comes more from talking with her than from the book. She has this phrase, that data is the "north star" of the field, and she said it long before scaling laws made it fashionable. But what I found in conversation is that she doesn't think of data as a resource you harvest. She thinks of it as a way of seeing. ImageNet was really a hypothesis about how children learn, about the sheer volume of visual experience a toddler gets, translated into something a machine could consume. That's a cognitive-science argument wearing an engineering costume. When I talk with her about what comes after language models, about spatial intelligence, about world models, the conversation never starts with architecture. It starts with "what does a human do, and what are we missing?" I've tried to adopt that habit. Before I ask how to build something, ask what the world actually looks like from the perspective of the agent you're trying to build.

The third thing is more personal. She's very open in the book about doubt, about feeling like an outsider, about not knowing whether she belonged in physics or in computer science or in America at all. There's a tendency for senior people in our field to project total confidence, and she doesn't. I found that useful, because I came to the US from China as well, and there's a version of this career where you spend all your energy trying to prove you deserve to be in the room. Her book quietly says that the uncertainty isn't a weakness to be hidden. It's actually where the curiosity comes from. The people who are sure they already understand intelligence don't build ImageNet.

And the last thing, which I think is underrated, is her insistence on the human side of all this. "Human-centered AI" can sound like a slogan. But when you talk with her, she genuinely does not separate the question of what we can build from the question of who it's for and what it does to people. She started that institute at Stanford before it was fashionable, and before most of us thought the technology would matter enough to warrant it. She was right earlier than she needed to be, again. I don't always agree with every position, but I've come to respect that she keeps asking the question, and that she asks it as a scientist rather than as a critic standing outside.

So, to summarize: patience for unpopular ideas, starting from how humans actually see rather than from what's convenient to build, honesty about doubt, and never losing track of the people on the other end. Those are the four things. The rest of it, the specific technical lessons, I think I would have gotten from the papers anyway. What the book and the conversations gave me is harder to get from papers.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Li’s experiences and openness about doubt were useful and relatable, but does not state that hearing stories from her past comforts Xie when he faces his own dilemmas and challenges.

astra-6.text:
What stays with me is the connection between the person and the scientist. We often talk about research as a sequence of ideas and results, but the questions someone chooses to pursue also come from their experiences, their values, and the people who have supported them.

For me, the takeaway is to step back from the immediate pressures of research and ask: Why does this problem matter? Who might benefit if we solve it? You can be deeply ambitious about the science while keeping those human questions in view.

And that also shapes how I think about mentorship. Helping someone become a researcher is more than helping them get a paper published. It’s helping them develop the confidence and judgment to find their own questions.

sol-6.1.text:
What I take away is that you can learn from someone’s path without trying to reproduce it. An autobiography gives you a coherent story, but in conversation, you can ask about the uncertainty behind the decisions—what wasn’t clear at the time.

For me, that’s a useful way to think about my own career, too: less emphasis on having every step planned out, and more on developing the judgment to choose what’s worth working on.
